analysis.one_liner: Bans civilian handgun ownership and sales, with exceptions for police, the military, guards, and licensed target clubs.
analysis.headline: The Senate never voted on the bill; after introduction in May 1993 and six rounds of floor remarks by its sponsor through February 1994, it sat in the Judiciary Committee until the 103rd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made it illegal for regular people to make, sell, buy, or own handguns or handgun ammunition, with exceptions for the military, police, registered security guard companies, and members of licensed target-shooting clubs. It offered a government buyback: anyone turning in a handgun within 180 days would get at least $25 or the gun's market value, while turning one in later would avoid prosecution but draw a fine of up to $500. The bill never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: People exposed to handgun violence, whose risk the bill targeted directly: the bill's findings cite record handgun homicides since 1987 and at least $4 billion a year in emergency, hospital, and rehabilitation costs from handgun injuries [S3]. Taxpayers would share in reduced health care spending if those injuries fell [S3]. Police, the military, registered security guard services, and members of licensed target-shooting clubs would have kept legal access to handguns under new licensing and storage rules [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Would have banned the manufacture, sale, purchase, ownership, possession, and transport of handguns and handgun ammunition by the general public, aiming to cut handgun homicides and injuries that the bill's findings link to $4 billion a year in health care costs
Would have paid at least $25, or the gun's fair market value, to anyone who voluntarily turned in a handgun within 180 days of enactment
Would have allowed people to surrender handguns to designated law enforcement agencies at any time without criminal prosecution, with only a civil penalty of up to $500 after the grace period
Would have required licensed handgun clubs and registered security services to store handguns securely, report losses or thefts within 30 days, and keep records open to federal inspection

analysis.who_pays: Existing handgun owners, who would have had to give up guns they already owned or face criminal penalties after a 180-day grace period, and later deliveries would have drawn a civil penalty of up to $500 [S3]. Gun and ammunition manufacturers, importers, and dealers would have lost most of the civilian handgun market, retaining only sales to police, the military, registered security firms, and licensed target clubs [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: Tens of millions of Americans already owned handguns legally, and the bill would have made continued possession a crime punishable by up to five years in prison and a $5,000 fine, falling on individual owners rather than on manufacturers or sellers
The buyback paid only $25 or fair market value, and a person who surrendered a gun after the 180-day window would still owe a civil penalty of up to $500, so late compliance carried a cost

The exceptions carved out large continuing handgun markets for police, the military, registered security firms, and licensed clubs, whose transfers would have remained legal under Secretary of the Treasury approval

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: If enacted, the bill would have attacked the leading instrument of U.S. homicides and hundreds of millions in annual injury costs, but by the bluntest means available: criminalizing possession for the roughly 70 million handguns the bill itself counted in private hands, with a modest $25-or-market-value buyback and prison exposure for owners who kept their guns. Gun owners who saw their property as lawful and their safety tool would bear the cost directly, while the promised safety gains depended on near-universal compliance that a voluntary buyback was unlikely to produce. It was an ambitious public-health proposal with a heavy, concentrated burden on individual owners and the gun trade.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee and then its Constitution subcommittee, and no one ever brought it up for a hearing or a vote before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Judiciary Committee on May 5, 1993, the day it was introduced
On June 24, 1993, the committee referred it to its Subcommittee on Constitution, where it stalled
The sponsor delivered introductory remarks on the floor at least six more times between June 1993 and February 1994, but the bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote in either chamber
The 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995, and the bill died with it

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Existing handgun owners, who faced no new restrictions or buyback requirements, and the firearms industry, which kept its civilian handgun market. No one who would have benefited from the ban got anything, because the bill never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Handgun owners and the gun industry

for.name: Sen. John H. Chafee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor repeatedly over nine months, from May 1993 through February 1994

for.name: Sen. Claiborne Pell
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's sole cosponsor at introduction

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Senate Judiciary Committee and its Subcommittee on Constitution
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral on May 5, 1993, sent it to the Constitution Subcommittee on June 24, 1993, and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or floor vote before Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the sponsorship was bipartisan but tiny, one Republican sponsor (Chafee) joined by one Democratic cosponsor (Pell).

industries.industry: Firearms and ammunition manufacturers, importers, and dealers
industries.note: The bill would have ended nearly all civilian handgun and handgun-ammunition sales, leaving the industry only a narrow regulated market serving police, the military, security firms, and licensed clubs. Industry interest in keeping the civilian market runs against the bill's public-safety goal.

Target-shooting clubs would have become the only civilian channel for legal handgun possession, requiring $25 annual licenses, secure on-site or police storage, and recordkeeping. Becoming a licensed gatekeeper would entrench them even as the bill regulated them.
Security firms would have kept the right to arm guards under a new $50 federal registration with storage and training rules, making them a recognized, licensed exception to the civilian ban.
